Insight: The dataset covers 18,265 daily observations across 5 cities from 2015-01-01 to 2024-12-31.
Cleaning removed no rows: the supplied file contains no duplicate records and no missing values, so the analysis rests entirely on originally recorded values.
Mumbai has the highest average AQI (318.185) and Chennai the lowest (316.619), a gap of 1.6 index points.

Although city averages differ slightly, the difference between cities is NOT statistically significant (ANOVA F=0.0985, p=0.983), so this dataset does not support a claim that any one city is materially more polluted.
PM10 shows the strongest association with AQI (Pearson r=0.2296, weak, p=4.49e-217); 3 of 9 pollutants reach significance at 0.05.

Measured linearly, PM10 explains only 5.3% of AQI variance, and correlation is not causation: this dataset contains no activity or meteorological data that could support a causal claim. A non-linear test (below) shows whether the near-zero Pearson coefficients really mean 'no relationship'.
K-Means was run with K=2, selected because it maximised the silhouette score (0.0838); the elbow rule suggested K=4.

The silhouette score of 0.0838 is below the conventional 0.25 threshold for meaningful structure, so the clusters should be read as a software partition of the value range rather than as naturally distinct pollution profiles.
Isolation Forest flagged 914 of 18,265 records (5.0%) as statistically unusual; Chennai contributes the most (200).

Anomaly rates differ across cities by only 0.87 percentage points, which is consistent with the configured contamination rate rather than with city-specific unusual events. Anomaly labels describe statistical unusualness, not an identified cause.
The best model by macro-F1 is Random Forest (accuracy 99.28%, macro-F1 0.7765).
The best model beats the prior-based baseline by +69.17 percentage points (30.11% -> 99.28%), so the pollutant columns do carry substantial information about the AQI band.

Leakage control applied: AQI_Bucket is derived from AQI, so AQI was removed from the predictors. Adding it back changes accuracy only from 99.28% to 99.96% (0.68 pp) - because the pollutant concentrations already recover the index almost completely.

AQI is almost fully determined by the pollutant concentrations: a cross-validated random-forest regressor reaches R2=0.9969 (MAE 1.2114) while linear regression reaches only R2=0.0579. The relationship is therefore strong but NON-LINEAR, which is why the Pearson matrix shows near-zero coefficients - a textbook warning against concluding 'no relationship' from correlation alone.

Because AQI can be reproduced from the concentrations with R2=0.9969, AQI behaves as a derived column in this file rather than as an independently measured quantity. Findings that compare AQI against pollutants are therefore partly circular and are labelled as such.

Greedy search identifies the columns AQI is built from: PM2.5 (0.4935) -> PM10 (0.9588) -> O3 (0.9862). PM2.5 alone reaches R2=0.4935, adding PM10 raises it to 0.9588, and every further column together adds only 0.0274 - so AQI in this file is computed mainly from the particulate-matter columns rather than measured independently.

The mean AQI profile across deciles of PM2.5 rises and then falls again (monotonic: False). A physical AQI sub-index cannot decrease when a concentration increases, so this relationship is arithmetically reproducible but not physically meaningful - the project reports it as an integrity finding instead of an 'insight' about pollution. Inside narrow PM2.5 x PM10 cells AQI still varies by 26.77 points on average (76.5% below the overall SD of 113.89), so a small residual comes from the other columns.

Insight: Integrity finding: 8 of 10 measured columns are statistically indistinguishable from a uniform distribution on a round maximum (all with excess kurtosis near -1.2 and near-zero skew), which is the signature of randomly generated values, not of monitored pollutant concentrations (real concentrations are right-skewed).
AQI over 2015-2024 shows a fitted slope of 0.0366 index points per year with p=0.9001: no statistically detectable trend. The dataset therefore does not evidence a rising or falling pollution trend.

Overall: the analytical pipeline is valid and fully reproducible, but the conclusions it can support are limited by the dataset itself. Patterns that real air-quality data shows (city ranking, winter spikes, PM-AQI coupling) are absent here, so they are reported as absent rather than asserted.
